No rows of seats, no projector, no wall. The audience watches from the driver's seat of a parked Tesla.

The film is Revolt, an AI-hybrid short we made, and this month it goes in front of Tesla, IMDA and a room of media. Instead of booking a theatre, we asked a simpler question. What is the most immersive private cinema most people already own? For a lot of them, it is sitting in their carpark. Two screens, seventeen speakers, doors shut, the world locked out.

I spent a call this week with Kaz from Tesla and Jaze, working out how you turn a showroom of cars into a cinema. It sounds absurd until you say it out loud. Then it sounds obvious.

This is the part of the job I love most right now. Not only making the film with AI, but questioning the whole ritual around it. The story stays sacred. Everything around the story is up for grabs.

Ten years ago I was a poly kid shooting corporate videos for anyone who would pay. This week I am turning Teslas into theatres with a government agency in the room. The work keeps getting stranger, and I keep saying yes.

Curious where AI film and new formats are heading in this region? DM me. Ten years in, and I am still on a shoot floor for a burger.

Food content is deceptively brutal. A burger has maybe a ninety second window where it looks like the thing you actually crave. After that the bun sags, the sauce dulls, the whole frame dies. So you build the entire day around those windows, which turns a schedule into a countdown.

That is knowledge you cannot brief into someone on the morning of. It lives in a team that has shot this a hundred times.

Everyone assumes AI takes days like this first. Anyone who has stood on a food set knows why it will not. The generated burger can look flawless and still feel like nobody was hungry when they made it.

AI carries our backgrounds, our cutdowns, our first passes. The hot food, the real steam, the timing, the hunger, that stays human.

Lean company. Long shoot days. Still the best part of the job.

If you are working out what to hand AI and what to protect, DM me. Not to open it. To give it back.

Reinstatement, disposal, rollers, a skip. Nobody posts this part of running a company. You see the launch photos. You never see the closing ones. Every lean business I admire has a room somewhere it quietly walked away from.

James and I stripped the place back to how we found it, throwing out gear that felt essential the day we signed the lease. Something is clarifying about carrying your own past out to a dumpster.

I have done this at a bigger scale. Fifteen staff down to one. It taught me the thing I keep relearning: overheads are never neutral. Every fixed cost makes you a little more cautious, a little more defensive, a little more likely to say yes to work you should refuse just to feed the machine.

Giving up a space is choosing what the next version of the company needs, instead of paying rent on what the last one did.

The company gets lighter. The decisions get braver.

If you are clinging to a lease, a tool or a team shape because letting go feels like going backwards, DM me. Worth saying out loud, because I spend my days advising founders on how to run leaner and use AI, and there is an unspoken assumption that the person giving the advice has it all figured out.

I do not. I have blind spots I cannot see, by definition. That is the entire point of a coach.

Huiyan Pan - Career Big Sis has told me things about my delegation and my time management that I did not want to hear and badly needed to. The most expensive lesson of my career came from her. My real bottleneck was me, holding on to decisions I should have handed over years earlier. Not the workload I kept blaming.

Nine sessions in, here is the pattern. The problems are rarely new. They are the same three habits, showing up wearing different project names.

Founders will spend thousands on tools. Far fewer will pay someone to sit across from them and say the hard thing to their face.

If you are the smartest person in your own company and it is starting to show, get a coach before you buy another subscription.

I turned up somewhere in the middle, got about ninety seconds with them, and they looked at me like I was the first person they had seen all day.

At my first Malay wedding, I walked out thinking about discipline.

They were up at four to pray, before a single guest existed. Then the ceremony, the performances, and hours of blessings, running until two or three in the afternoon.

The blessings move fast. That is the format. Guests come up, take the moment, take the photo, make way for the next family. A river of people, and everybody gets their minute.

Which means the couple gave that minute several hundred times over. The same warmth to the last person as to the first, eleven hours in, starting at four.

I have produced enough long days to know what that costs. Anyone can be present once. Being present on the four hundredth repetition, when your feet hurt, and you have been performing since dawn, is a completely different skill.

To my friend Aisah, congratulations. Thank you for letting me sit in on something I had never seen Gives you a sense of how far your content spread.","value":69,"unit":"count"}],"metricsUpdatedAt":"2026-09-08T12:13:40.082Z"}},{"cursor":"WkRFM09EVTRNRFV5TURBd01EQT06YVRaaE5tWTVOVGczWVdGalpESTBNV05tWkdGbVlXTTRPUT09","node":{"id":"6a6f9587aacd241cfdafac89","status":"sent","allowedActions":["viewPost","sharePostLink","copyPostLink","updatePostTags","addPostNote","duplicatePost","updateShopGridLink"],"via":"buffer","text":"On the twenty ninth I sat in a cinema watching Spider-Man have an identity crisis, and recognised the problem immediately.

Sony invited me to the premiere of Brand New Day. No spoilers. Go and watch it, because Marvel and Sony have put the narrative back at the centre where it belongs.

The part I keep turning over is that the villain is barely the point. The real fight happens inside one person, with Peter deciding which version of himself he is allowed to be.

I ran that same argument for years. Creative or commercial. The guy who makes beautiful work, or the guy who reads the P&L. I treated it as something I had to settle, kept picking a side, and quietly resented whichever one I put down.

Cutting Tristeps from fifteen staff to one settled it for me. I could not afford to be only a creative. I also could not afford to stop being one, because taste is the only thing a one person studio genuinely sells.

So I stopped choosing. The work got better and the margins got better in the same year.

Most founders I meet are stuck in that argument. The creative who thinks selling is beneath them. The operator who outsourced taste years ago and cannot work out why everything went flat. Both are waiting for permission to also be the other thing.

Right now I run a production studio and an AI consultancy at the same time, and people keep asking which one I actually am. Both. Each one pays for the other.

Green door, upstairs, ring the bell for Hannah. That is the kind of detail a recce is made of. Where the light falls at 3pm, whether the aircon hum ruins the audio, how many people you can fit up a narrow staircase without it becoming a fire hazard.

The film itself is the interesting part. We are narrating it twice. English in a calm third person, Mandarin in first person, in the talent's own voice. Not a subtitle, not a dub. Two emotional registers for two audiences, inside the same film.

Most brands treat a second language as a checkbox. But a story lands differently in English than it does in Mandarin. The rhythm changes. The intimacy changes. First person in Mandarin pulls a viewer close in a way a neutral narrator never can.

It might be the most useful conversation I have had in months.

The question on the table was simple. When did play become unproductive?

As children, play was the most natural thing in the world. No goal, no metric, no point to prove. Somewhere on the way to becoming adults, we turned it into something we have to schedule, justify, or earn. We made play productive, which is almost a contradiction in terms.

I got deep into it with Steph and Daemon, ex-Ergotune, and Daemon shared something that reframed the whole evening for me.

Growing up, his father loved to talk. Mostly his own opinions, often about how great China is. Young Daemon kept offering his own views back, not realising his dad was never asking for them. His father wanted to be heard, full stop.

For years, talking to his dad was hard. Then Daemon flipped it. Instead of fighting for airtime, he started asking his father more, prompting him, seeing how far he could take him. He turned a frustrating dynamic into a quiet game, a challenge to draw his dad out.

Years later, he realised that was a form of play. The adaptive kind, where a child finds a way to connect on the only terms available to him.

That sat with me for the rest of the night. Play is how we stay flexible when life refuses to give us what we want. It is bigger than fun.

I run hard most weeks. Rooms like this remind me that the most productive thing I can do is sometimes to stop trying to be productive.

When did you last play with no point to it at all? Three rounds forces better decisions earlier. The client thinks harder before each note. We protect the idea instead of sanding it down to please everyone.

Worth every minute, period.

It was the World Cup watch party, USA against Paraguay, hosted at the Embassy here in Singapore.

The football was the easy part to enjoy. 

The part that caught me was watching a country build its brand in real time. A World Cup is the biggest stage on earth, and a nation that uses it to gather people, tell its story, and earn goodwill is running the same playbook the sharpest brands run. Sport is simply the most powerful medium anyone has found to carry it.

That is the work I think about every day, here on a smaller scale.

I also got to meet some of the people who make these rooms happen. Jessie and Hazizah Osman from the Embassy's Press and Media team on the Public Diplomacy side, and Jorim Kok from FleishmanHillard. Sharp, generous with their time, and genuinely good company, and most importantly, good food.

New faces, a rare room, and a quiet reminder that saying yes early and showing up in person is still one of the most underrated moves in business.

Grateful for the invite. Mornings like this are exactly why I show up.

When we were growing, my partners hired people they could manage from day one.

People who needed direction. Who needed checking in on? Who needed approval before moving?

They called it building a team.

What they were actually doing was building a support system for themselves.

And I get it. Hiring someone more capable than you is uncomfortable.

It means you can't hide behind knowing more.

It means you have to lead, not just oversee.

But here's the thing about hiring people you can babysit: you'll spend all your time doing exactly that.

The business won't grow. Your time won't free up.

You'll just become a very expensive day carer for adults who were never set up to win.

The hires that changed Tristeps were the ones I wasn't sure I deserved.

People who brought something I couldn't replicate.

People who made me sharpen up just to stay relevant in my own company.

Hire people who make you better.

Everything else is just filling seats.

Most business partnerships fail not because of market conditions or bad timing.

They fail because two people with different beliefs about what the company should become stayed together too long after the belief stopped being shared.

I've been there.

I spent years managing a partnership that looked functional from the outside and felt broken on the inside.

The direction one person was excited about, the other was tolerating.

The decisions that took twice as long because the conviction wasn't equal on both sides.

The vision that slowly became one person's burden instead of two people's ambition.

I saw the signals early.

I chose not to look. Not because I was naive. Because I was afraid of what it would mean if I did.

Ending or restructuring a partnership is not a failure.

It's one of the hardest things a founder can do, and it's often the thing that saves the company.

The question I now ask before committing to any working relationship:

What do you want this to become in 5 years? And what are you not willing to do to get there?

The gap between those two answers tells you everything.

Most of us skip the question entirely.

That's the expensive part. 

Shoutout to my partner-in-crime, James, who is one of the few left and the one who always stuck by me through these 10 years.

I chose business partners the way most people choose: whoever was there, whoever I trusted in the moment, whoever seemed aligned enough to get started with.

I didn't say product. Didn't say pricing. Didn't say market timing.

I said: who you go with.

Partner misalignment doesn't announce itself. It accumulates.

It shows up in the decision you can't quite align on. The direction one person is excited about and the other tolerates. The vision that starts to belong to one person more than both.

I scaled Tristeps from 15 staff to 1 full-time person.

Revenue doubled. Revenue per employee went up 15x.

Everyone called it smart. Efficient. Brave, even.

What nobody told me is what comes after the subtraction.

The fear of adding again.

Because once you've proven you can run lean - once you've felt the clarity of a small, precise operation - every hire feels like a risk.

Every new person is a new belief system to manage. A new direction to align. A new relationship where the shared objective can slowly drift.

I've lived through what happens when that drift goes unchecked.

So the idea of building a team again, even a small one, carries weight it didn't used to.

I know what can break.

That's not a reason not to grow.

But it is a reason to grow differently.

This time I'm building the architecture before I build the team.

The systems, the culture, the values - explicit before anyone joins.

The foundation has to exist before the people arrive.

Not the other way around.

"How did you start your business?"

I'm 31. I've run a production company for over 10 years. We've worked with Google APAC, Sony SEA, McDonald's Singapore. At 25, I made my first million.

They expected me to say: spot the gap, take the leap, figure it out as you go.

I said: get your foundations right before you do any of that.

The room went quiet.

Your tertiary years are the last time in your life you get to train how you think, with low stakes.

The cognitive muscle you build then - structuring problems under pressure, managing people who frustrate you and still delivering, holding two opposing views and working out which one holds - that muscle is what business will test, relentlessly, for the rest of your career.

I had a business partner who was brilliant in the room but fell apart under pressure.

I had another who was loyal until the direction changed.

Neither of those situations ended well.

What made the difference, in both cases, was not my product knowledge or my client relationships.

It was how clearly I could think when everything around me was unclear.

I kept partners who had already mentally checked out.

Different circumstances. Same lesson.

We were both paying a price for something that wasn't working - and telling ourselves it was temporary.

Gavin's version cost him his marriage. Mine cost me a near-payroll crisis, $10K a month on an office three people barely used, and a period where I was running the vision alone without admitting it out loud.

The moment he stopped driving was the moment everything changed.

I stopped too. Cut the team. Cut the office. Went from 15 people to one.

Revenue doubled.

The business didn't need more. It needed me to stop adding things that weren't working and actually commit to what was.

Gavin built an 8-figure company after his 18 months.

I'm still building. But I finally stopped confusing motion with progress.

Swipe through his story. Some of it will feel familiar.

"If you want to do this, I'll follow you. But this isn't what I want."

I kept going.

I told myself: That's just how partnerships work. Not everyone has to be equally excited about every direction.

What I didn't hear was the real message.

They were already out.

In their head. In their energy. 

In the room.

That sentence was the ending of a chapter I hadn't finished writing yet.

I should have stopped and had the harder conversation right then.

What do you actually want to build?

Is this still the same company we both signed up for?

Are we still going the same direction?

Instead I kept moving. They stayed put.

And I called that alignment for another eighteen months.

If someone in your business says "I'll follow you but this isn't for me," take it seriously.

That's not support. 

That's an exit with extra steps.

He still left saying he didn't feel valued.

That wasn't a compensation problem. That was someone who had already decided to leave and needed a story to justify it.

I watched it happen slowly. Small things first. Commitments that slipped. Conversations that went sideways. Decisions that didn't add up.

I told myself it was a rough patch. It wasn't.

Gavin Sim said something in our conversation that I wish I had heard five years earlier.

"If you don't show integrity in the small things, you won't show it in the big things. When someone shows me a lack of integrity, I walk away."

The version of me that kept giving chances and adding resources, hoping the situation would turn around - he needed to hear that.

Money doesn't change people. It amplifies them. If the small things were already off, more resources just make the exit more expensive.

You stop moving. 

You start consulting.

You stop leading.

Founders say this like it's something to be proud of.

I used to.

But there is a second half to that phrase most people forget.

"Jack of all trades, master of none BRO"

Taking every brief, every format, every client who walks through the door feels like a hustle. 

It feels like maximising opportunity.

What you're actually doing is building a business that stands for nothing.

And a business that stands for nothing is very easy to replace.

At Tristeps, we used to do events, commercials, marketing, social, and anything to keep the doors open.

We said yes to all of it.

And we became expensive generalists.

The moment we got specific, the right clients found us faster.
Pricing got easier.

The work got better.

You can die trying everything and be good at nothing.

Pick the one thing you are genuinely exceptional at.

Build your whole identity around it.

Let the rest go.

No dancers. No pyrotechnics. No costume changes.

Two years ago, he was reportedly on the edge of financial collapse. Cancelled his world tour. Sold his entire music catalogue, 290 songs, for $200 million just to stay afloat. Lost his manager. Disappeared.

Then he came back. New albums. Grammy nomination. And the biggest crowd Coachella has ever seen.

I watched that set and felt something I recognised.

At 27, I made my first million running a creative agency in Singapore. At 30, I was the only one left standing. Most co-founders out. Team dissolved. A $10K/month office that two people barely used.

Everyone told me to hire. Scale back up. Fill the gaps.

I did the opposite.

Cut the office. Cut the ego. Scaled down to one staff member and rebuilt every system from scratch.

Revenue doubled. We landed Google APAC & 3M Asia. 15x revenue per employee in 18 months.

I call it The Subtraction Principle.

When things break, most founders reach for more. More people, more tools, more noise. The sharper move is usually to strip back to what actually works and let everything else go.

Bieber proved it on a stage. I proved it in a business.

Four steps inside the carousel. Swipe through.

If you have ever had to rebuild from nothing, I would genuinely like to hear your version. Drop it below.

I'm Henry. I run Tristeps Studios, and I'm building a show called Founders Notes for founders who are still in the room, still figuring it out, and tired of pretending they have it all sorted.
